# Add Security Consideration for Client Metadata Changes

**Summary**: The specification could benefit from a brief security consideration noting that client metadata documents can change over time, which authorization servers should consider when implementing caching and grant management policies.

## Current Specification Language

From [Section 6.3 Changes in Client Keys](https://drafts.aaronpk.com/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document.html#name-changes-in-client-keys):

> If the authorization server notices that the `jwks_uri` or the contents at the `jwks_uri` have changed compared to the last time it fetched the metadata, the authorization server MAY take actions such as revoking any tokens issued to this client, or revoking the user's consent for this client. The particular actions to take are left up to the discretion of the authorization server based on its own risk assessment.

This addresses key changes but doesn't mention the broader implications when other metadata fields change.

## Rationale

Client metadata documents are served from URLs under client control and can be updated at any time. While [Section 4.3 Metadata Caching](https://drafts.aaronpk.com/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document.html#name-metadata-caching) provides HTTP caching guidance, authorization servers should consider the security implications when other fields change as well.

For example, changes to `redirect_uris` could potentially enable redirect hijacking if not properly validated, modifications to `token_endpoint_auth_method` change the authentication security model, and updates to `scope` or `grant_types` could affect the authorization scope of existing grants. Even changes to display fields like `client_name` or `logo_uri` could be part of client impersonation attacks.

This isn't about defining specific policies, but raising awareness that metadata mutability beyond just keys is something authorization servers should consider in their risk assessments.

## Recommendation

Adding a brief paragraph to [Section 6 Security Considerations](https://drafts.aaronpk.com/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document.html#name-security-considerations):

> **Changes in Client Metadata**
>
> Authorization servers should be aware that client metadata documents can change over time since they are served from URLs under client control. Beyond the key changes addressed in Section 6.3, authorization servers should consider the security implications when other metadata fields change, such as `redirect_uris`, `token_endpoint_auth_method`, `scope`, `grant_types`, or display fields like `client_name` and `logo_uri`. 
>
> Significant changes to client metadata may affect the trust relationship between the authorization server and the client, and could impact the validity of previously granted user consent. Authorization servers may choose to invalidate existing grants, require fresh user consent, or implement other policies when certain types of metadata changes are detected. The appropriate response will depend on the authorization server's risk tolerance and operational requirements.

## Related Work

- Builds on the existing guidance in [Section 6.3 Changes in Client Keys](https://drafts.aaronpk.com/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document.html#name-changes-in-client-keys)
- Complements the HTTP caching guidance in [Section 4.3 Metadata Caching](https://drafts.aaronpk.com/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document.html#name-metadata-caching)

## Implementation Impact

This adds minimal text while raising awareness of an important security consideration. It doesn't prescribe specific behaviors but helps implementers think about metadata mutability in their designs.

issues.author: identitymonk
issues.body:
I think there are two DOS risks on the authorization endpoint (and other endpoints that could accept CIMD as parameter) that might worth spelling it out in the security section of this specification:

- I could force through multiple authorization requests to an AS with CIMD hosted at a slow responding endpoint mobilizing resources at the AS up to a DOS situation

** Proposed text **
```
Client ID Metadata Document Fetch DOS

Authorization servers fetching client metadata documents SHOULD implement appropriate rate limiting and timeout mechanisms
when retrieving Client ID Metadata Documents. A malicious actor could attempt to cause a denial of service by initiating multiple
authorization requests using a client_id that points to an intentionally slow-responding endpoint, potentially exhausting authorization server resources.

Authorization servers SHOULD implement measures from this non exhaustive list:
- implement standard anonymous and bad reputation IP filtering, as well as DNS name filtering
- Implement strict timeouts when fetching metadata documents
- Rate limit requests per client_id URL and/or requesting IP
- Consider caching valid responses as specified in Section 4.4
- Terminate requests that exceed reasonable response times
```

- I could force through multiple authorization requests to an AS to fetch what could be CIMD at 3rd party, mobilizing resources at this 3rd party up to a DOS situation

** Proposed text **
```
Third-Party Endpoint DOS Protection

Authorization servers MUST take precautions to prevent their metadata document fetching mechanism from being used as an
amplification vector in DOS attacks against third-party endpoints. A malicious actor could attempt to use the authorization
server's metadata fetching capabilities to direct high volumes of requests to an arbitrary third-party target.

Authorization servers SHOULD implement measures from this non exhaustive list:
- implement standard anonymous and bad reputation IP filtering
- Implement per-endpoint rate limiting for metadata document fetches
- Monitor for patterns of repeated requests to the same endpoints
- Consider maintaining allow-lists and deny-lists of trusted domains for metadata documents
- Implement circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures
```

issues.author: aaronpk

An AS can decide what it considers the security boundary client identity. For example, an AS can decide that the domain name is the security boundary of the client, and any path variations on the domain are considered the "same client" for purposes like auto-approving previously authorized OAuth grants.

e.g. `https://example.com/client/v1.json` `https://example.com/client/v2.json` could be considered different versions of the same client.

The AS may want to take various factors into account, like only considering the domain the boundary for trusted domains, to avoid domains commonly used for hosting services like azure that are shared across multiple customers.

comments.body:
Actually this is what `software_id` in the client registration vocabulary means. So maybe we could use that:

```
{
  "client_id": "https://example.com/client/v1.json",
  "software_id": "https://example.com/client.json"
}
```

There would need to be a way to link back from `https://example.com/client.json` to `https://example.com/client/v1.json` otherwise it doesn't solve the problem of the overlap on shared domains.

Any new actual mechanism should probably be done as a separate extension. But I thought it would be worth pointing out non-normatively in security considerations that an AS might want to have its own policies around domain trust, similar to other things mentioned about domain trust.

fwiw this came up from a discussion with someone who was hoping to be able to publish updated metadata like the redirect URI but keep the client ID value the same to avoid an AS revoking tokens and prior user consent.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body:
I'm a fan of opt-in additional metadata fields within the CIMD over a new meta-client document. Or a new `software_id` document - `software_id` is also currently defined as an opaque string, not a URL — so there's no way to dereference it and link back to the clients that claim it. 

What if we built the bidirectionality directly into CIMD with a root/instance model? (naming... to be improved on?)

Root document — the canonical client identity. A complete CIMD document that additionally declares URL patterns for deployments it considers part of the same logical client:
```
  {
    "client_id": "https://example.com/client.json",
    "client_id_type": "root",
    "client_instance_patterns": [
      "https://example.com/client/v*.json"
    ],
    "client_name": "My App",
    "redirect_uris": ["https://example.com/callback"],
    "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
  }
```

Instance document — a complete, fully standalone CIMD document that additionally declares a relationship to a root:
```
  {
    "client_id": "https://example.com/client/v2.json",
    "client_id_type": "instance",
    "client_root": "https://example.com/client.json",
    "client_name": "My App",
    "redirect_uris": ["https://example.com/callback2"],
    "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
  }
```
An instance document is a fully valid CIMD document on its own. The `client_id_type` and `client_root` fields are additional metadata. An AS that doesn't understand root/instance ignores those fields and processes the document normally — it just sees a regular client.

An AS that does support the extension can:
1. Fetch the instance, note the `client_root`
2. Fetch the root, confirm the instance's `client_id` matches a pattern in `client_instance_patterns`
3. Treat the instance as the same logical client as the root for purposes of consent, grants, and admin allowlisting

Both sides must agree — the instance claims a root, and the root's pattern list confirms the claim. The AS may want to verify that some security-critical fields are consistent between the two - the same way the AS needs to handle metadata changing in `6.3.  Changes in Client Metadata` today.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body:
Dialing back the solutioning a tad from my last comment:
- I agree with @ThisIsMissEm's comment from October that the trust boundaries should be explicit. If trust boundaries are implicit and defined by the AS, then the same client (or... set of CIMD documents) can be parsed and treated differently by different ASs and we will get interoperability issues.
- I think that the existing CIMD document is the best place to define the trust boundary, instead of creating a new meta-document or software-statement structure

comments.body:
I think we could establish links between clients without the need for an additional meta-client, `software_id`, or root client document. #67 suggests adding guidance around how clients can identify versions of themselves, and we could build on that:

<details>

<summary> (example collapsed for space) </summary>

```diff
{
    "client_id": "example.com/client/prod-v1.0.json",
    "software_id": "example.com/client/prod",
    "software_version": "v1.0",
+   "next_software_version": "v1.1"
}

{
    "client_id": "example.com/client/prod-v1.1.json",
    "software_id": "example.com/client/prod",
    "software_version": "v1.1",
+   "prev_software_version": "v1.0"
+   "next_software_version": "v1.2"
}

{
    "client_id": "example.com/client/prod-v1.2.json",
    "software_id": "example.com/client/prod",
    "software_version": "v1.2",
+   "prev_software_version": "v1.1"
}
```

</details>

This allows for a couple of things:
- The client can use `software_id` to indicate a _minimum_ trust boundary, i.e. "even if an AS treats different versions as part of the same client, it MUST NOT treat different `software_id`s the same."
  - This also allows for multiple independent client version chains, e.g. the client can have another `software_id: example.com/client/dev` that has different capabilities and perhaps localhost redirects.
- The client can present a trust chain within that boundary as a suggestion to the AS, i.e. "`v1.2` is just a new version of the same software."
- The AS can use all of that information to decide if it wants to:
  - Treat different `client_id`s as different clients
  - Treat different `software_id`s as different clients
  - (some third option)

> keep the client ID value the same to avoid an AS revoking tokens and prior user consent

At the end of the day, I think this is entirely up to the AS, but I do agree that the client should be able to indicate what should happen.

@ThisIsMissEm, this slightly modifies my thoughts in #67 -- I'll add a comment there indicating that :)

issues.title: Add a mechanism for client-triggered early metadata retrieval
issues.author: TakahikoKawasaki
issues.body:
While authorization servers can calculate the lifetime of client metadata using the methods described in [RFC 9111 HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html) and continue to reuse the retrieved metadata until the calculated expiration time is reached, client applications may sometimes want authorization servers to re-fetch the metadata before that expiration time.

Could we introduce a mechanism that allows client applications to trigger such early metadata retrieval? For example, what about introducing a new request parameter like `cimd_max_age`, similar in concept to the `max_age` parameter defined in [OpenID Connect Core 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html)?

This issue is related to PR #29 "Improve documentation for development usage and expiration of clients", I think.

comments.author: panva
comments.body: Just prescribing to use a "max-age" HTTP Response Header would probably be cleaner than introducing a new server metadata.

comments.author: TakahikoKawasaki
comments.body:
@panva Thank you for your comment.

This is not a proposal to introduce new server metadata, but rather a new runtime request parameter.

I implemented CIMD with a caching mechanism that leverages existing HTTP semantics, including `max-age`. However, I still believe that having a mechanism to trigger earlier metadata retrieval would be beneficial.

[OpenID Federation](https://openid.net/specs/openid-federation-1_0.html) defines the `trust_chain` request parameter. When included in an authorization request, it instructs the authorization server to update the client metadata using the provided trust chain, even if the cached trust chain has not yet expired. I hope that CIMD can also offer a similar mechanism to trigger early metadata retrieval, analogous to the `trust_chain` request parameter.

issues.title: Clarify jwks vs jwks_uri support
issues.author: yissellokta
issues.body:
The Problem
Section 4.1 pulls in jwks via the DCR registry, but Section 6.3 only discusses rotation/updates for jwks_uri. This leaves the expected behavior for embedded jwks unclear.

The Proposal
I suggest we only support jwks_uri for CIMD and disallow embedded jwks.

Reasons:
- Reduced Complexity: For Dynamic CIMD, the Authorization Server (AS) shouldn't have to re-parse the entire metadata document just to find a key change.
- Clean Invalidation: Invalidation is much cleaner when the cryptographic identity is hosted at a separate jwks_uri rather than inside the metadata.
- Existing Patterns: Current implementations already focus on jwks_uri for dynamic rotation.

**Question**
Does the group see a hard requirement for keeping jwks embedded, or can we move to a jwks_uri only model to simplify implementation?

issues.author: MichaelFraser99
issues.body:
The draft's text includes the following stipulation:

```
Client identifier URLs SHOULD NOT include a query string component
```

Given query strings are inherently unordered, this leads to the scenario where client identifier comparisons using strict string comparison may fail for two URLs that are still semantically the same. As such, I believe we should explicitly ban the use of them to reduce ambiguity.

Additionally, it's worth noting that OpenID Federation 1.0 (referenced by the document as another example of Client Identifiers being URLs) explicitly bans Query parameters in this location so aligning for interoperability may also be valuable.

issues.author: MichaelFraser99
issues.body:
[OpenID Relying Party Metadata Choices](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-rp-metadata-choices-1_0.html) introduces a set of metadata for a scenario where an RP needs to advertise support for a set of metadata that itself is a single-value claim. Such metadata is intended to be used where an RP _may_ support multiple different options for a given claim such as `token_endpoint_auth_method` that a given ecosystem or domain may support.

While nothing in this document explicitly prohibits this, an implementation consideration would be valuable here. 

Perhaps some text akin to:

```markdown
In a deployment where a given Client may be expected to interact 
with servers that support multiple different options for single-value 
claims, the claims registered in the [OpenID Relying Party Metadata Choices](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-rp-metadata-choices-1_0.html)

```

issues.title: Define AS behavior when CIMD contains unsupported metadata values
issues.author: panva
issues.body:
CIMD Section 4.1 client metadata values are those from the DCR Metadata registry but doesn't say what an AS should do when the document contains values the AS doesn't support - for instance a `grant_types` entry like `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` on an AS that doesn't offer DAG.

Both RFC 7591 and OpenID Connect DCR explicitly permit the AS to either reject or substitute/filter unsupported metadata. RFC 7591 says the AS "MAY reject or replace any of the client's requested metadata values [...] and substitute them with suitable values" and that the client can then "check the values in the response to determine if the registration is sufficient for use."

That last part is key - DCR has a negotiation step. The client sends requested metadata, gets back what the AS actually registered, and decides whether it can work with that. Both behaviors (reject or filter) are fine because the client gets feedback.

CIMD doesn't have this (by design). The client publishes one static document for all ASs. There's no response for the client to inspect. Without guidance in the spec, AS implementers may default to the stricter DCR behavior (reject), either by choice or unknowingly by reusing the DCR client metadata validations, which is at odds with clients having a single general purpose static document.

Example: VS Code publishes `https://vscode.dev/oauth/client-metadata.json` with `grant_types` including `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, and `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`. An AS that supports CIMD but not DAG may reject the whole thing, even though `authorization_code` would work fine.

The spec could say that when processing a CIMD, the AS should filter array-valued fields like `grant_types` and `response_types` to the intersection of what the client declares and what the AS supports, and must reject only when that intersection is empty. This is consistent with what DCR already allows - it just makes filtering the expected default for CIMD, which makes sense given the lack of a negotiation step.

But the remaining issue is the potential lack of upfront knowledge. Especially for client metadata related to AS metadata that is defined as optional such as grant_types_supported. Note that I now realize grant_types_supported does have a default specified when omitted.

So I wonder if, combined with the prescribed non-eager reject behaviour, select AS metadata without a default should in addition be made REQUIRED when used in combination with CIMD so that the client knows (or at least can infer) what the resulting metadata likely is that the AS will use. (note I didn't give much thought into scouring each metadata definition for a list just yet)

Refs: https://github.com/panva/node-oidc-provider/issues/1398

comments.body:

+1

In general I'm a fan of making more required fields. It's easy for developers to copy-paste default values into their config. It can be hard to deal with the ambiguities around missing values.

Also does CIMD say anywhere what the AS should do with unknown metadata fields (not just values)? DCR says it MAY ignore, filter, or reject them, but I think the lack of negotiation in CIMD means that the AS MUST ignore all unknown field values. This enables clients to add extra fields that they know some AS will read (as this will surely happen in practice).

issues.title: Ambiguity around `application_type` when metadata defaults and usage patterns point to different client types
issues.author: btiernay
issues.body:
## Summary

The CIMD specification does not appear to say how `application_type` should be handled when it is omitted and therefore defaults to `"web"` under [RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591), but the client uses redirect URI patterns described in [RFC 8252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252) for native applications.

This seems relevant because RFC 8252 also says that redirect URI alone is not enough to distinguish client type, and that the client type needs to be recorded during registration so the authorization server can determine how to treat the client.

That leaves some uncertainty around how CIMD is expected to interact with existing OAuth guidance on client type.

## Problem Description

CIMD reuses the OAuth Dynamic Client Registration metadata model from [RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591). In that model, `application_type` is client metadata, and if it is omitted, the default value is `"web"`.

At the same time, [RFC 8252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252) describes redirect URI patterns used by native applications, including loopback redirect URIs. It also says that redirect URI alone is not sufficient to distinguish a public native app from a confidential web client, and that the client type is required to be recorded during client registration.

This creates a question when:

- `application_type` is omitted, so the RFC 7591 default is `"web"`, and
- the client uses loopback redirect URIs associated with native apps in RFC 8252

## Example

Consider a client that:

- omits `application_type`
- uses loopback redirect URIs such as `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://localhost`

Relevant specifications:

- [RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591)  
  If `application_type` is omitted, the default is `"web"`.

- [RFC 8252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252)  
  Loopback redirect URIs are described for native applications, but redirect URI alone is not enough to determine client type, and the client type is required to be recorded during registration.

In that situation, it is not clear how CIMD expects an authorization server to treat the omitted `application_type`:

| Possible reading | Possible result |
| --- | --- |
| Apply the RFC 7591 default strictly | The recorded client type is `"web"` |
| Treat the configuration as incomplete for RFC 8252 purposes | The client metadata is insufficient until client type is explicitly recorded |

CIMD does not currently seem to say how this case should be understood.

## Interoperability Impact

If different implementations handle this differently, the same client configuration may be accepted in one environment and rejected in another.

This appears to have practical relevance in deployed systems, for example:

- [anthropics/claude-code#18251](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/18251)
- [anthropics/claude-code#37747](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/37747)

Possible effects include:

- inconsistent handling of clients that omit `application_type`
- uncertainty about whether the RFC 7591 default is sufficient in RFC 8252 scenarios
- reduced interoperability across implementations

## Question

When `application_type` is omitted and therefore defaults to `"web"` under RFC 7591, but the client uses loopback redirect URIs described in RFC 8252, is that default intended to be sufficient for recording client type, or is explicit client type metadata expected?

## Motivation

Clarifying this would make it easier to understand how CIMD relates to RFC 8252’s requirement that client type be recorded during registration, especially in cases where `application_type` is omitted and the RFC 7591 default may not reflect the intended client type.

https://www.iana.org/assignments/oauth-parameters/oauth-parameters.xhtml#client-metadata

> The client metadata document is a JSON ([RFC8259]) document containing the metadata of the client. The client metadata values are the values defined in the OAuth Dynamic Client Registration Metadata OAuth Parameters registry ...

If the answer is yes then the interoperability question still exists, just with a different citation chain. If the answer is no, then CIMD probably needs a clearer OAuth-native way to express the same client-profile information.

issues.title: Mixup attacks with issuer identifiers
issues.author: erincandescent
issues.body:
Picture this scenario:

* `example.com` run an AS which implements this spec
* `example.net` also run an AS with issuer identifier `https://example.net/`. 
* `example.com`'s AS is also connected to `example.net` as a client 

If an attacker can place a JSON file at `https://example.net/`, they can use it as a client ID. They can then use the client credentials grant and potentially (depending upon which OAuth 2 extensions are implemented by `example.com`) will mint JWTs with `{"iss":"https://example.com","sub":"https://example.net"}`.They may be able to trigger flows which result in minting OpenID Connect ID tokens `{"iss":"https://example.com","aud":"https://example.net","sub":"usersub"}`. These ID tokens may then be abusable with e.g. the JWT bearer authorization grant, e.g. via the identity chaining spec. 

It may seem unlikely that an attacker can place a JSON file at the root of `https://example.net/`, but consider a setup where a frontend proxy has the configuration:

* `https://example.net/.well-known/` -> forwarded to IDP. The other endpoints of the IDP might live on e.g. `https://auth.example.com/`
* `https://example.net/` -> forwarded to a Wordpress installation with insecure plugins

This attack can be relatively silently executed. The attacker can modify the code at `example.net` to sniff if the request is coming from a web browser (inferable because the user agent starts with `Mozilla`, or because `text/html` is in the accept header, or similar) and return the usual home page, only returning the client ID metadata to clients that look like an AS.

There are three potential ways I see of avoiding this:

1. Embed the client metadata inside the AS metadata document. This makes the `oauth-authorization-server` name misleading (though `openid-connect` less so), but it absolutely guarantees the two entities with the same URI are actually the same entity (In retrospect it might have been better for it to be `/.well-known/oauth` with properties under e.g. `"as"`, `"rp"` and `"rs"`, but that ship sailed a long time ago)
2. Place the client metadata in `/.well-known/oauth-client` and trust that `.well-known` is well controlled. This is probably OK. There may be a hazard here between OAuth and OpenID style uses of `.well-known`...
3. Proceed as is, write several paragraphs of guidance in the Security Considerations section cautioning people about potential for confusion between client IDs and AS issuer IDs and watch as everyone gets it wrong and we create a new rich mine of security vulnerabilities

issues.author: njwatson32
issues.body:
The draft says:

```
The authorization server MUST NOT cache error responses.  The
authorization server also MUST NOT cache documents which are invalid
or malformed.
```

I think there need to be allowances for short-lived negative caching to avoid:

1. Spamming unrelated websites with calls (#30)
2. Exacerbating outages with repeated requests

issues.title: Can AS optionally provide `iss` when fetching client_id?
issues.author: njwatson32
issues.body:
For example, if `client_id=https://example.com/oauth/client_id.json`, the AS would `GET https://example.com/oauth/client_id.json?iss=https://example-as.com`.

This allows the client to do a few things:

Progressive rollouts of changes to CIMD, so that blast radius is limited to only certain AS. Making a global change to a client id is bad practice from a production safety point of view, and "random percentage" rollouts may not work if the AS queries the CIMD more than once and gets two different documents.  Of course, `iss` isn't a perfect solution here, but it's easy and better than nothing.

The client could also return AS-specific metadata (as long as it's not secret because `iss` is unvalidated). This could help address certain incompatibilities that may arise in practice where the same values are rejected by some AS but not by others.

comments.author: ThisIsMissEm
comments.body:
This goes against the nature of CIMDs, which is explicitly to not be variable, they're meant to be static files. 

> Client identifier URLs SHOULD NOT include a query string component

An AS issuing a `GET /oauth/client_id.json?iss=https://as.example` would be getting a different document, a different client_id from `GET /oauth/client_id.json` since the URL must strictly match the client_id

comments.author: ThisIsMissEm
comments.body: CIMDs also do not know anything about their AS's, they are just presenting data to an AS when the AS requests it. They shouldn't know the difference.

comments.author: njwatson32
comments.body:
> Client identifier URLs SHOULD NOT include a query string component

As written in the draft, this refers to the URL the _client_ presents, not the HTTP GET request made by the AS.  Analogously, redirect URIs shouldn't contain query strings either, and must strictly match a registered value, but obviously the AS attaches parameters when it redirects there. It's the same idea here.

> they're meant to be static files.

This is an implementation detail up to the client.  Indeed, clients aren't required to do anything with `iss`. They are free to ignore it and serve a static file if they want.

> CIMDs also do not know anything about their AS's

They still don't have to.  This proposal builds in a piece of flexibility that is sure to be necessary at some point. Authorization servers already have serious problems updating AS metadata, and the same will be true of CIMD. Having an `iss` parameter would allow something as simple as a gradual rollout of a change that's sticky on AS (e.g. `return hash(iss) % 100 <= rollout_percent ?  new_cimd : old_cimd`.) It's also a near certainty that authorization servers will have different policies (or bugs) that make a CIMD work with one and not with the other, so an `iss` parameter gives a client (who is so inclined) the opportunity to correct that.

I would phrase the language as:

```
The authorization server SHOULD include an `iss` parameter when fetching client_id,
which clients MAY use to modify the results of the document. The `client_id` field in
the document MUST be equal to the client_id URL _without_ the `iss` parameter.
```

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
I think the key issue is not “different ecosystems.”

The harder problem is that even a single ecosystem is operationally heterogeneous during rollout, migration, experimentation, and recovery. Modern SaaS systems are almost never upgraded atomically.

That matters because CIMD changes can directly affect interoperability and protocol behavior.

For example, a client may begin enabling DPoP, PAR, JAR, or private_key_jwt, while only some AS deployments in the ecosystem support it yet.

Without per-iss metadata:

* the CIMD changes globally
* every AS immediately sees the new metadata
* older or partially upgraded ASs may reject or mishandle it

With per-iss metadata:

* upgraded ASs receive the new metadata
* older ASs continue receiving compatible metadata
* rollout can proceed incrementally with isolated rollback and reduced blast radius

I do not think “just publish a new CIMD URL” solves this cleanly because a new CIMD URL effectively creates a new client_id. **That turns deployment management into identifier management.**

Operators may end up creating:

* “stable” client IDs
* “beta” client IDs
* “dpop-enabled” client IDs
* rollback client IDs

even though the logical client has not changed.

Many of these rollout differences are temporary operational states:

* partial AS upgrades
* feature validation
* staged key rotation
* migration windows
* bug mitigation

Per-iss metadata treats compatibility as deployment state rather than client identity, which I think is the cleaner abstraction for progressive delivery within a single ecosystem.

A concrete enterprise failure mode here is partial rollout across a multi-region SaaS deployment.

For example, a client enables private_key_jwt or DPoP support in its CIMD. Some AS clusters in the ecosystem have been upgraded and support the new behavior, while others are still on the previous version due to staged rollout or rollback.

With a single static CIMD:
- upgraded ASs succeed
- older ASs may reject the client
- authentication failures appear intermittently depending on routing, region, or cluster
- rollback now requires reverting the global CIMD for everyone

That creates an ecosystem-wide blast radius from what should have been a controlled incremental deployment.

Per-iss metadata allows the metadata publisher to safely stage compatibility changes against specific AS deployments without fragmenting the ecosystem into separate client IDs purely for rollout management.

comments.author: ThisIsMissEm
comments.body:
CIMDs come from a decentralised world where there is no relationships between Authorization Servers and Clients, effectively a many-to-many ecosystem between clients and Authorization Servers.

They work around the short comings of DCR where in a many-to-many ecosystem, you end up with an explosion of client registrations of increasing complexity to manage for both the client and the AS.

If you have a relationship between the client and AS, why are you using a CIMD? Why not use a statically registered client with each AS? Alternatively, there is the option presented in the security considerations at the end of CIMDs-but-not-really where you use a URI for client_id but it's just statically registered with the AS (tbh, that section should probably be dropped)

Varying CIMD contents based on AS requesting it explicitly creates a relationship between clients and the AS's.

comments.author: matthieusieben
comments.body:
I tend to agree with @ThisIsMissEm here. If your purpose is to authenticate the AS towards the CIMD endpoint, this would be better done using an `Authorization` header which would contain a JWT bearer with the `iss` field you want.

I'd rather be discussing that than adding hard coded query string params to the spec, especially since the proposed iss params conflicts with the fact that the client id may (tho it should not) contain query params.

comments.body:
i think the upgrades/rollout problem might be better solved by versioning CIMD, which came up as a separate topic some time ago (alignment pending, see #55 and #67). i'm also not entirely sure that i follow this point @mcguinness :

> For example, a client may begin enabling DPoP, PAR, JAR, or private_key_jwt, while only some AS deployments in the ecosystem support it yet.

isn't this why we have AS metadata, so that ASes and clients can align on which features they both support and communicate appropriately? if a client looks at an AS's metadata and sees no support for `private_key_jwt`, i'd imagine it should not try to use a client assertion with that AS, much like an AS wouldn't expect a client assertion from a client that doesn't claim to support `private_key_jwt`s. perhaps i'm missing something here?

> Operators may end up creating:
>
> - “stable” client IDs
> - “beta” client IDs
> - “dpop-enabled” client IDs
> - rollback client IDs

to me, each of these should correspond to a separate client ID (or at least a separate version or software ID). if i am an AS, i might want to distinguish between stable/prod and beta clients for the same underlying app, because these clients may pose different security considerations.

more to the point, i'm not a fan of codifying in this draft any request metadata that the AS is expected to send in a CIMD request. the client, when identifying itself to an AS, knows enough about the AS to provide a different client ID altogether if it really wants to, which i don't think is currently _prohibited_ by this draft. if a client wants to call itself `client.dev/mcp-client.json` when connecting to an MCP server and `client.dev/atproto-client.json` otherwise, that is the client's discretion and the AS doesn't have to be involved.

comments.author: ThisIsMissEm
comments.body:
For something like `token_endpoint_auth_method` currently the client metadata can only present a single option, `private_key_jwt` or `none` or one of the other registered auth methods. This makes sense in DCR perhaps, but maybe for CIMD we would actually need an array of supported values by the client.

So instead of negotiating the CIMD based on the AS, and having:

```
// legacy AS requests and gets:
{
  "client_id": "https://client.dev/oauth/metadata.json",
  "client_name": "client.dev",
  "client_uri": "https://client.dev",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://client.dev/oauth/callback"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
}

// modern AS requests and gets:
{
  "client_id": "https://client.dev/oauth/metadata.json",
  "client_name": "client.dev",
  "client_uri": "https://client.dev",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://client.dev/oauth/callback"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt"
}
```

you'd be saying, all AS's get the same metadata about the client, but the client can present multiple values, so, regardless of which AS requests, you'd get:
```
{
  "client_id": "https://client.dev/oauth/metadata.json",
  "client_name": "client.dev",
  "client_uri": "https://client.dev",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://client.dev/oauth/callback"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": ["none", "private_key_jwt"]
}
```

And then the client during PAR or Authorization Requests would specify the exact value for `token_endpoint_auth_method` to use for that grant.

comments.author: ThisIsMissEm
comments.body: (I'm not sure how that'd work with DPoP though, due to it being a boolean value, a `dpop_bound_access_tokens: [false, true]` would be kinda weird)

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
> token_endpoint_auth_method currently the client metadata can only present a single option
> I'm not sure how that'd work with DPoP though, due to it being a boolean value, a dpop_bound_access_tokens: [false, true]

This is getting to the root of my feedback. CIMD is currently publishing configured values and not just supported capabilities by reusing client registration metadata params that was originally intended as part of a single client registration (configured values).  Change management of these values is very risky as currently defined.   A CIMD publisher can't just publish a new capability is supported without changing the configured value which may have broad impact across the ecosystem.

comments.author: njwatson32
comments.body:
I strongly agree with Karl's statement:

> I do not think “just publish a new CIMD URL” solves this cleanly because a new CIMD URL effectively creates a new client_id. That turns deployment management into identifier management.

Creating a new client id is going to have far broader implications in many cases, including invalidation of existing user consent. Suppose a client starts out with a single global CIMD https://client.example.com, and then a year later it wants to modify its config for AS1. If it starts passing https://client.example.com/as1 to AS1, AS1 will treat this as a brand new client_id which will force all users of the client to consent again.

And if you're not changing the client_id, all you can do is change the contents of the document, and clients need a safe way to deploy such changes.

> If you have a relationship between the client and AS, why are you using a CIMD? Why not use a statically registered client with each AS?

Because you might already be using CIMD in your deployment, including with that AS, and switching client ids to a statically registered one could be disruptive. This also doesn't address the global config change blast radius problem that CIMD has as written.

Even if CIMD is updated to reflect client capabilities rather than configured values, global config changes are still problematic. AS Metadata is proof of this, as it has arrays of supported values and still runs into trouble when making "backwards compatible" updates (https://www.hyrumslaw.com/). Building in support for `iss` from v0 provides a harmless (clients can ignore it if they want) piece of flexibility.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body: Per-issuer CIMD documents would also enable a client to reveal a unique callback URL per-issuer, which is one of the mitigation strategies for issuer mix-up attacks.

comments.author: ciamshrek
comments.body:
I think a slightly different use-case here might for something like SingPass, or Highly Controlled Ecosystems, where its required to use a different signing key. Right now since CIMD exposes a single `jwks_uri` it also ends up requiring us to generate urls as 

```https://example.com/connection/<unique_name>/oauth/client.json```

Which IMO is suboptimal to

```
https://example.com/oauth/client.json
```

issues.title: Review from Justin Richer
issues.author: ThisIsMissEm
issues.body:
Just so we don't loose his comments in the [mailing list](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/DRzDT8q_j3PaGwoEJEpgZwcyccI/), I'm copying them here below, we'll probably want to review these separately or split them out into separate issues later:

---

Overall:

I think this is missing a discussion on the kinds of clients where this approach makes sense, and where it does not. Namely, if a client is relatively well-known and has an established home, like a website, then this works great. For other clients, including those in §4.2, it's not as great a fit. I think it's fine for this specification to not work for a class of clients - and it should be upfront about it instead of pretending it fits well.

§3

This feels like it should be a list, not a paragraph. Try reformatting and see if that works?

Globally redefining "client identifier" seems a bridge too far for this spec to do in isolation, consider perhaps defining "Client Identifier URI" or something specific to CIMD so as not to imply that ALL client identifiers are now URLs.

Refer to the URI spec (RFC3986) for URI parts. The "username or password" is called the "userinfo" subcomponent of the authority, for example. And "port" is also part of the authority.

"Port" should probably have some matching done to it — like defaults of 443 being equivalent to non included — or it should be direct string comparison only as implied by §4.1 and default port processing expressly disallowed. Really, leaning on the URI definitions will help this too.

"This specification places no restrictions" after a bunch of restrictions is … weird. Perhaps be more specific about what "no restrictions" are included in "no restrictions" like URL shorteners or stability. That said, most shorteners use redirects to work, which breaks the resolution restriction in §4, can we square that circle?

§4

It's not clear why fetching the document is a "should". I know it can be associated by hand, so I think maybe that's what this SHOULD is trying to get at. Perhaps call out that it MUST be associated with a set of client metadata, which is available at the URL, and the AS SHOULD fetch it automatically within security considerations.

§4.1

"The client metadata document MUST be served with a 200 OK HTTP status code" this is a requirement of the fetch process not the document.

Does "the URL of the document" mean the URL used to fetch the document, exactly? This sounds like it's something the AS (fetcher) needs to validate, then — call out both of these more explicitly.

Suggest that the discussion on client secrets be pulled out as a separate section to highlight its importance here. Also add discussion on private keys, but public keys are allowable.

I see no discussion of software_Statement and how it would fit with this work, suggest we add discussion of how (or if) they fit together. I personally think they could be layered with some cautions on the trustworthiness of the software_statement (since it's no longer presented inline by the client).

Suggest that you separate the "what's in the doc" from "how you get the doc" in this section overall.

§4.2

While I see the practical appeal, the CIMD-service really just feels like a weird way to do static registration but use a side door to do so. This also seems like it directly contradicts the trust model proposed by this specification. I would recommend removal of this beyond discussion in security considerations, or add it as an appendix to describe how CIMD-as-a-service could be built and offered by a party, and discuss the security and reputation implications thereof.

§4.3

What if the server isn't fetching it, under some circumstances allowed by §4? Are there any validation requirements (that might need its own section alongside 4.1)

§4.5

By "exact match" I assume this means string-match, either call that out or point to the logic in the core OAuth specs that say so.

This also implies that only redirect-based grants are allowed to be used, but I don't see that called out anywhere in here. Could I use CIMD for client_credentials or token exchange? Device flow? CIBA? Why or why not?

§6

Generally speaking, there shouldn't be any normative text in security considerations. Especially the MAYs here are pointless and more explanatory than requirement anyway. Stick to non-normative text in this section and put the normative requirements further up.

§6.5

"except when the authorization server itself is also running on a loopback address and the resolved address matches the same loopback interface" — couldn't this be used to force an AS to call a loopback function from the outside via a client-provided value? I'm failing to see what the use case to allow this cutout is. Development is a different world where restrictions like this are routinely relaxed, but here it reads like this should be a normal cutout for the protocol.

§6.6

"Authorization servers SHOULD limit the response size" — how does the AS limit the size of a file it does not control? Do you mean limit processing to the first 5k and erroring or discarding the rest?

§6.8

Suggest adding a discussion of allowlists, especially of domain patterns — eg, "anything from [foo.com](http://foo.com/)". The framing of different policies for different states of client trust is a good one, keep that.

§6.9

This doesn't seem like a security consideration, but an implementation consideration.

More to the point, the AS needs to be able to differentiate between clients registered via CIMD and clients registered by other means. Client ID prefix is only one aspect of this, as there might be AS's that do use https:// for clients (such as vanity IDs or stable developer-facing identifiers), but don't fetch the data. Suggest calling out that "do I fetch this or not" is the key difference.

§6.10

This doesn't seem like a security consideration, but an implementation consideration. I would argue that it leverages the namespacing and other aspects of CIMD while not relying on automated systems — so I would suggest not framing it as "Defeating the purpose". This discussion could be helped by separating the "fetch" from "format" as suggested above.

§??

This is missing privacy considerations, please add them. In particular, AS fetching or providing to the end user any URLs dynamically handed over by the client in a CIMD could lead to leaking user usage patterns or information.

issues.title: Privacy Considerations Section
issues.author: ThisIsMissEm
issues.body:
> This is missing privacy considerations, please add them. In particular, AS fetching or providing to the end user any URLs dynamically handed over by the client in a CIMD could lead to leaking user usage patterns or information.

This comes from Justin Richer's review (#79), and it is a section we should probably cover. We already have a bunch of security considerations around URLs in CIMDs, but we don't yet have a privacy considerations section. I think this would be an extension of the text in [Dynamic Client Registration](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7591#autoid-23), however, this specifically would not apply:

> Note that clients are forbidden by this specification from creating their own client identifier.

In CIMDs the client does indeed control the document URL and therefore the `client_id`, so could theoretically use those for tracking purposes. I think I've even seen some people attempting this, which lead to some of the restrictions on redirects and other security considerations.

issues.title: Section 4.5 Redirect URIs
issues.author: ThisIsMissEm
issues.body:
Also from #79, Section 4.5 specifies some language for Redirect URIs, https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-redirect-url-registration

We may want to consider aligning this text with OAuth 2.1's text: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1#section-4.1.1-28

> In particular, the authorization server MUST validate the redirect_uri in the request if present, ensuring that it matches one of the registered redirect URIs previously established during client registration ([Section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1#client-registration)). When comparing the two URIs the authorization server MUST ensure that the two URIs are equal, see [Section 6.2.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-6.2.1) of [[RFC3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc3986)], Simple String Comparison, for details. The only exception is native apps using a localhost URI: In this case, the authorization server MUST allow variable port numbers as described in [Section 7.3](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252#section-7.3) of [[RFC8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8252)].

Or specify it in a way that directly references the normative model for redirect URIs and registration / validation of them.

comments.author: localden
comments.body:
+1. We hit this in practice with Claude Code's CIMD client metadata: at least one implementer (FastMCP, before PrefectHQ/fastmcp#3589) read the current Section 4.5 wording as unconditional exact-match and rejected ephemeral-port loopback redirects from a native client whose `redirect_uris` were registered portless per RFC 8252 Section 7.3. Their fix cited 7.3 directly, but Section 4.5 gave them no hint the exception applied.

One thing worth making explicit alongside the OAuth 2.1 text: the "native apps" condition in that exception ties to `application_type` (per RFC 8252 Section 8.4), which connects this to #75. A client metadata document that omits `application_type` defaults to `web`, so an authorization server reading the proposed text strictly wouldn't apply the loopback exception unless the document sets `application_type: "native"`.

issues.title: Add guidance for pattern-based Client ID Metadata Document URL admission policies
issues.author: anoopgarlapati
issues.body:
## Summary

[Section 6.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-client-id-domain-trust) describes heuristic trust decisions (for example, reputation systems or user warning flows) while [Section 6.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-pre-registering-client-id-m) describes exact URL pre-registration of Client ID Metadata Document URLs. The specification does not currently discuss deployment models where authorization servers apply administrator-configured policies based on URL patterns, such as domain allowlists or path-prefix restrictions.

Some enterprise deployments require admitting Client ID Metadata Document URLs based on trusted origins or URL namespaces without requiring exact enumeration of every permitted URL.

## Motivation

### Dynamic-path Client ID Metadata Document URLs

Some deployments generate distinct Client ID Metadata Document URLs per integration or per protected resource while maintaining a common origin and URL structure.

For example, [OpenAI's developer documentation](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/auth) describes ChatGPT-originated flows using Client ID Metadata Document URLs of the form:

* `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/github/client.json`
* `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/example/client.json`
* `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/<server>/client.json`

In this model, the authorization server may wish to admit Client ID Metadata Document URLs under a trusted path namespace such as `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/*` without requiring exact pre-registration of every possible URL.

This deployment pattern is not directly addressed by either [Section 6.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-client-id-domain-trust) heuristic trust evaluation or [Section 6.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-pre-registering-client-id-m) exact URL pre-registration.

### Implementation Experience

Related deployment models and implementation mechanisms have appeared in multiple implementations and proposals, including:

* administrative trust configuration for CIMD-enabled deployments
* domain-based trust policy configuration in MCP ecosystem implementations
* [MCP SEP-991](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/991) discussion of protected-server trust models based on trusted domains or specific clients.

Providing guidance in the specification may improve interoperability and reduce divergence in deployment behavior.

## Proposed Change

Add a subsection under [Section 6.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-client-id-domain-trust) describing pattern-based admission policies for Client ID Metadata Document URLs.

Proposed text:

> Authorization servers MAY apply admission policies to Client ID Metadata Document URLs based on URL patterns rather than requiring exact URL pre-registration as described in [Section 6.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-pre-registering-client-id-m).
>
> Such policies MAY include:
>
> * domain-based allowlists,
> * URL path-prefix matching, or
> * other administrator-configured policy mechanisms.
>
> For example, an authorization server might permit Client ID Metadata Document URLs under a configured namespace such as `https://trusted-client.example.com/oauth/*`.
>
> In enterprise or managed deployments, authorization server implementations SHOULD provide administrators with mechanisms to configure such policies.
>
> Authorization servers SHOULD evaluate these policies before retrieving the referenced metadata document in order to reduce unnecessary outbound requests and limit exposure to SSRF-related attack surfaces described in [Section 6.5](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-server-side-request-forgery).
>
> Pattern-based admission policies do not replace redirect URI validation requirements. Authorization servers MUST continue validating redirect URIs against the client metadata as described in [Section 4.5](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-redirect-url-registration).
>
> The syntax and matching semantics of pattern-based policies are outside the scope of this specification.

comments.author: ThisIsMissEm
comments.body:
In a recent review it was noted that security considerations should generally be non-normative rather than normative text. Current we list these as part of the normative text.

My understanding of section 6.10 is actually that they're onboarding a specific CIMD URL and the exact version of that document, such that live fetching isn't happening, @aaronpk knows more about this specific deployment pattern.

There are parts of section 6 that need to be moved up to normative sections, but you can already do what you're proposing if you want (I think).

That said though, having multiple CIMDs can be an anti-pattern, especially if it allows user tracking, though obviously you'd likely need a CIMD per ecosystem supported (or the server would need to discard invalid scopes)

comments.author: anoopgarlapati
comments.body:
Thanks @thisismissem, this is really helpful — and the 6.10 framing in particular is something I'd misread. Responding to each of your points:
**_On normative vs. non-normative in 6._** Understood and that changes my ask. I'm not trying to add new MUST/SHOULD/MAY requirements into Security Considerations. My proposal works as a descriptive guidance. Happy to drop the normative keywords from the proposed text and frame it as an acknowledgement of an observed deployment pattern, with the SSRF and redirect-URI points moved to references back into 6.5 and 4.5 where the actual normative requirements already live.
**_On 6.10._** Thanks for the clarification. I had been reading 6.10 as "exact-URL pre-registration with live fetching" (effectively just a narrower admission policy), but you're describing something stronger such as onboard a specific CIMD URL and freeze the document contents at onboarding, with no further fetching. If that is the intent, it would help to make that explicit in 6.10's text, because today the section doesn't actually say fetching stops. It just says the URL can be pre-registered. (I wouldd be glad to propose a small clarifying tweak to 6.10 separately if @aaronpk confirms that's the intent.)
Either way, that's a different model from what I'm describing. My case is live fetching of a CIMD document whose URL is admitted because it matches an administrator-configured origin (or namespace) i.e., the metadata can still change over time, 6.3 still applies, and 6.4/6.7 still matter for consent UI. That's neither 6.10's frozen-snapshot model nor 6.8's per-request heuristic. It is an admission decision applied before section 4 discovery happens.
**_On "you can already do this."_** Agreed that nothing in the spec forbids it. The reason I think a short acknowledgment is still worth adding is interop: two deployments are already shipping this pattern with different assumptions about what redirect-URI validation, metadata caching, and consent-UI behavior should look like once a CIMD URL is admitted by pattern rather than enumerated. A non-normative paragraph that says "this deployment model exists, and when used, 4.5 and 6.5 continue to apply unchanged" would cost little and head off the divergence.
**_On the multi-CIMD anti-pattern._** This is a fair point and worth calling out in any text we add. A publisher serving distinct CIMD URLs per protected resource does produce distinct client_ids, which the AS will see per-user and could correlate (or be made to correlate). I'd suggest the descriptive text include a sentence flagging this — something like: "Publishers that serve many CIMD URLs under a common origin should be aware that each distinct URL is a distinct client_id from the authorization server's perspective, and may have user-tracking or consent-fragmentation implications. Scope handling across such clients is at the discretion of the authorization server." That keeps the anti-pattern visible without prescribing a remedy the WG hasn't agreed on.
Revised, non-normative text (intended as a short paragraph appended to section 6.8):

> Some deployments admit Client ID Metadata Document URLs by matching against an administrator-configured set of trusted origins or URL namespaces, rather than enumerating each permitted URL as described in Section 6.10. This is an admission decision that occurs before the discovery step in Section 4, and is distinct from the per-request heuristics described in Section 6.8. The matching algorithm and its configuration are out of scope of this specification; implementers matching on URL components beyond the origin should be aware of the pitfalls described in [RFC9700], Section 4.1.3.
When such an admission policy is used, the metadata document is still fetched and validated as described in Section 4, and the redirect URI validation in Section 4.5 and the SSRF mitigations in Section 6.5 apply unchanged.
Publishers serving many Client ID Metadata Document URLs under a common origin should be aware that each distinct URL is a distinct client_id from the authorization server's perspective, with corresponding implications for user tracking and consent fragmentation.

If that framing works, I'm happy to open a PR. And, separately, if @aaronpk can confirm the "freeze the document at onboarding" reading of 6.10, I'll send a second small PR clarifying that section, since it would help disambiguate the two patterns.

issues.title: Add `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` to client metadata
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Currently, RFC8414 defines `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` as "JSON array containing a list of client authentication methods supported by this token endpoint". (Even though this is referred to as token endpoint, this actually applies to client authentication at other endpoints such as the PAR endpoint.) This enables an AS to declare which client authentication methods are supported, so a client can choose which to use.

DCR defines `token_endpoint_auth_method` as a single string, "the requested authentication method for the token endpoint". So a client can request a particular auth method when it registers, presumably from the list of supported methods at the AS.

Now in the world of CIMD, clients no longer register with an individual AS. Instead the AS discovers metadata about the client. This means `token_endpoint_auth_method` doesn't really work, because the client metadata document is not aware of the AS.

If we add `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` to the CIMD, the client can also advertise its supported auth methods. This would enable the negotiation to work both ways. The various combinations of client and AS support of `none` and `private_key_jwt` are below:

* Client supports both, AS supports both:
  * The client advertises support for both `none` and `private_key_jwt`. The AS advertises support for both `none` and `private_key_jwt`. When the AS fetches the client metadata, it sees the client supports both, and can reject requests with no auth.
* Client supports `none`, AS supports both:
  * The client advertises support for only `none`. The AS fetches the client metadata and sees only `none`, so accepts no auth.
* Client supports `private_key_jwt`, AS supports both:
  * The client advertises support for only `none`. The AS fetches the client metadata and can see that the client supports `private_key_jwt`, so can require auth and block other clients from using the CIMD URL without authentication
* Client supports both, AS supports `none`
  * The client would not send any client auth, and the AS accepts it because it can see the client also supports `none`
* Client supports both, AS supports `private_key_jwt`
  * The client would see the AS requires auth, the AS accepts it because it can see the client supports `private_key_jwt`

Without this ability to negotiate, you can end up in these not-desirable situations:

* The client advertises `token_endpoint_auth_method: "private_key_jwt"` but an AS that only supports `none` rejects that CIMD URL because it doesn't see `none` as the value.
* The client doesn't advertise any `token_endpoint_auth_method`, so the AS is forced to accept both `none` and `private_key_jwt` for that CIMD URL
* The AS is unable to enforce `private_key_jwt` for clients that support it

For these reasons I believe we should add `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` to the client registration vocabulary established by DCR.

issues.title: Requiring ASes to return the `iss` parameter for mix-up prevention
issues.author: itsvs
issues.body:
Pulling out an idea from #78 into a separate thread as there are some competing thoughts there. One of the reasons mentioned for clients using per-issuer CIMD documents is in order to enable mix-up prevention by providing distinct redirect URLs per AS ([comment](https://github.com/oauth-wg/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/issues/78#issuecomment-4502302325)). The tradeoff is that clients no longer have a single document to represent them, which somewhat goes against the static nature of CIMDs.

As an easier way to enable mix-up prevention, we could require that ASes that build CIMD support also include the `iss` parameter in the response redirect, as suggested in [[WG Draft] OAuth 2.1 Section 7.14.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-15.html#section-7.14.1). Pulling this requirement into the CIMD draft would ensure that ASes don't have to implement all of 2.1 just to enable mix-up prevention, and clients could use this method rather than per-AS CIMD documents.

issues.title: Security Consideration: discourage clients from using dynamic CIMD documents
issues.author: itsvs
issues.body:
As noted in #82, some implementations of CIMD involve dynamic client paths being used to render CIMD documents. The specific scenario in that issue is probably fine, but currently there is not much preventing an implementation from allowing something like a dynamic/unvalidated (e.g.) `?redirect_uri=[...]` parameter, and it could be pretty bad if a client's CIMD could be dynamically configured to include a custom redirect URI, custom JWKS URI, etc.

The draft states that document URLs "**SHOULD NOT** contain a query component," but since this is not a "**MUST**", implementers may well ignore the recommendation. It may be prudent to include a security consideration to discourage use of unvalidated query parameters to configure a document at runtime.

Acknowledging that clients may implement multiple CIMD documents for a variety of valid reasons, this mainly boils down to ensuring that the documents that a client exposes are _intentional_ -- e.g. if a client _must_ expose different documents with different JWKS URIs, the client should intentionally specify paths for the documents rather than use a dynamic path like `example.com/<jwks-uri>/client.json`.

issues.title: privacy and security risks of inconsistent client metadata
issues.author: npdoty
issues.body:
Dynamic modification of the metadata seems like a new capability to attack users, by customizing metadata per user in order to mislead them, and not reveal the misinformation to other parties.

It seems like this is intended for publishing public documents at stable URLs, which would be beneficial for users trying to protect themselves -- they can access that metadata through a proxy; a researcher can check the contents of that data and try to detect abuse. But if the metadata is provided dynamically, like dynamically generated customized per user or per authorization server, then it's easier to track users who are interested in an oauth client's metadata and it's easier to mislead users by providing them different, misleading metadata.

It would be useful for privacy and security if we at least identified whether the metadata document was intended to be consistent (and if so, we could work on technical mechanisms for that). And if it's not intended to be consistent, then I think we should document the threats as a result, and what users need to do to protect themselves.

(The use cases where I'm thinking about this in particular are when a relying party is requesting verifiable digital credential presentations from a user's wallet. Some have suggested that client metadata would be the way to indicate privacy-relevant details, like privacy policies or usage commitments. But if that data is inconsistent, then it's more of a way to mislead users than a way for users to obtain reliable metadata.)

pulls.title: Add security consideration for logo_uri usage
pulls.author: ThisIsMissEm
pulls.body:
I'm not 100% happy with the wording here, but this does begin to address the concerns around displaying logos to end-users that are provided from within the client metadata document.

The idea is to provide a security consideration similar to the consideration in Dynamic Client Registration: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591.html#section-5

> In a situation where the authorization server is supporting open client registration, it must be extremely careful with any URL provided by the client that will be displayed to the user (e.g., "logo_uri", "tos_uri", "client_uri", and "policy_uri").  For instance, a rogue client could specify a registration request with a reference to a drive-by download in the "policy_uri", enticing the user to click on it during the authorization.  The authorization server SHOULD check to see if the "logo_uri", "tos_uri", "client_uri", and "policy_uri" have the same host and scheme as the those defined in the array of "redirect_uris" and that all of these URIs resolve to valid web pages.  Since these URI values that are intended to be displayed to the user at the authorization page, the authorization server SHOULD protect the user from malicious content hosted at the URLs where possible.  For instance, before presenting the URLs to the user at the authorization page, the authorization server could download the content hosted at the URLs, check the content against a malware scanner and blacklist filter, determine whether or not there is mixed secure and non-secure content at the URL, and other possible server-side mitigations.  Note that the content in these URLs can change at any time and the authorization server cannot provide complete confidence in the safety of the URLs, but these practices could help.  To further mitigate this kind of threat, the authorization server can also warn the user that the URL links have been provided by a third party, should be treated with caution, and are not hosted by the authorization server itself.  For instance, instead of providing the links directly in an HTML anchor, the authorization server can direct the user to an interstitial warning page before allowing the user to continue to the target URL

Perhaps the section should be also including `tos_uri`, `policy_uri` and `client_uri` (e.g., asserting that the Authorization Server can choose to validate the documents at these URIs and also choose whether or not to display these URIs to the end-user.

comments.author: trwnh
comments.body:
@aaronpk wrote:

> I am a bit rusty on media types but isn't there a way to say `application/cimd+ld+json` or something as a more specific media type than `application/ld+json` that is also compatible with `application/cimd+json`?

Relevant history:

- https://github.com/w3c/did/issues/208
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-mediaman-suffixes/01/
- https://github.com/w3c/did/issues/863
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-mediaman-6838bis/

In summary: DID work reached out to IETF about +ld+json as a potential structured suffix, and got a skeptical response in 2020. An RFC draft was filed to update the structured suffix registry in 2022, but after IETF review it was rejected and the RFC draft expired. There is now another draft RFC updating the structured suffix registry to disallow multiple suffixes:

> While it might be desirable to indicate multiple use cases simultaneously using a compound suffix (e.g., "+xml+zip"), experience shows that suffixes are a poor basis for this; the combinations of suffixes quickly multiply, and there is not a well-specified processing model that can handle them safely.  Therefore, multiple suffixes are disallowed from use.

It is possible for the DID work to have pursued something like `application/did+ld` or `application/did+jsonld`, but they ended up going with `application/did` instead. This pattern was adopted for Verifiable Credentials (VC) and Controlled Identifiers (CID) work as well, with `application/vc`, `application/vp`,  and `application/cid`.

## Multiple media types

Unfortunately, this creates a bit of a new quagmire: how do you signal or know when multiple media types apply? https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/#media-type-precision describes the concept of "media type precision": 

- application/vc and application/vp are the most specific types, indicating that Verifiable Credentials or Verifiable Presentations semantics and processing are in effect.
- application/ld+json is a less precise media type, indicating a Linked Data processing mode, with explicit semantics provided by the `@context`.
- application/json is even less precise, indicating JSON document processing and no in-band semantics. (Semantics are loaded out-of-band in the application layer.)
- text/plain is even less precise, indicating a plain-text processing mode that renders the content of the document verbatim as a UTF-8 sequence (or some other encoding).
- application/octet-stream is the least precise media type, indicating a processing mode where raw bytes are streamed in sequence.

So we can see that the best practice right now is to be as precise as possible, wherever feasible.

### JSON-LD and Solid-OIDC compatibility

Side note regarding JSON-LD: content type sniffing is also possible in some cases, such as detecting the presence of a `@context` key. However, the JSON-LD context may be missing, in which case applications using JSON-LD processing can make use of "context injection" to kinda convert the more specific types to `application/ld+json`, using out-of-band application knowledge/semantics to recognize which media types can be converted like this (and which contexts to inject): https://www.w3.org/TR/cid-1.0/#context-injection

Solid-OIDC specifically does not require any specific Accept type; it currently requires `application/ld+json` for the *response* only, and also makes an exception for content negotiation: https://solidproject.org/TR/oidc#clientids-document

> When a Client Identifier is dereferenced, the resource MUST be serialized as an application/ld+json document unless content negotiation requires a different outcome.

It seems like CIMD doesn't require the *response* to use `Content-Type: application/cimd+json`, which means for compatibility, the CIMD processor should probably be prepared to accept less precise media types such as `application/ld+json` or `application+json` 

## Summary

- Clients can always request the most specific type of `application/cimd+json`, to indicate that they are CIMD processors and intend to process the returned content as a CIMD document serialized in JSON.
- Servers should be prepared to respond to requests for `application/cimd+json`.
  - If the server supports negotiating for `application/cimd+json`, it can return 200 OK with the CIMD.
  - If the server has a default representation, it can return the CIMD as the default representation.
  - Edge case: the server might return 300 Multiple Choices for client-driven content negotiation. This should be recommended against.
  - Edge case: the server might return 406 Not Acceptable, if it strictly recognizes only certain content types as having representations. This should also be recommended against.
- Clients should be prepared to receive a less precise Content-Type in the response, and should not treat this as an error.
  - Potential security consideration for "raw" servers which accept user-generated content. These servers may use `Content-Type: text/plain` or `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` as an indication that the content should not be processed with more specific processing models. (I am not sure if this allows for CIMD-based impersonation, or if there are other security considerations that prevent this from being an issue.)

### Recommended language to add

- Something about serving CIMD documents as the default representation:
  > "The client metadata document MUST be the default representation when content negotiation is used. The HTTP server hosting the client metadata document MUST NOT use client-driven content negotiation (responding with HTTP 300 Multiple Choices). The HTTP server hosting the client metadata document also MUST NOT respond with 406 Not Acceptable."
- Something about clients not erroring out on other Content-Type values in the response:
  > "The HTTP server hosting the client metadata document might be configured to respond with a Content-Type other than application/cimd+json, so the Authorization Server MUST be prepared to process valid client metadata documents served with less precise media types. These less precise media types MAY include application/json or application/ld+json."
  - ...maybe briefly include a note about media type precision?
  - describe in more detail exactly when the document "conforms to `application/<AS-defined>+json`" 
    - btw you left a "`application/<AS-defined>+json`" in there, so replace that placeholder :)
  - is any +json suffix okay here?

pulls.title: Add `software_version` to identify metadata changes
pulls.author: itsvs
pulls.body:
The -01 draft suggests that clients should refrain from updating metadata too frequently, and that authorization servers should expect occasional changes to metadata. It might be helpful for clients to make it easy for servers to identify when metadata has changed.

RFC 7591 provides a `software_version` field that we could use for this purpose. This PR introduces a couple of recommendations along these lines:
- Clients may include this field to indicate when the metadata document has changed and/or to differentiate between application versions with different capabilities
- If clients parameterize this in the URL, authorization servers could treat different versions as different clients with different policies.

I briefly chatted about this with Aaron before making this PR, and I am very much open to discussing further!

comments.author: itsvs

Yes. Authorization servers may wish to enforce different policies based on client capabilities, so if those vary across client versions, the versions should be treated as different clients. Updating the same client wouldn't work since multiple versions of a client might exist at any given time (e.g. if users need to update the client app).

That being said, I don't think clients have to host _every_ new software version at a separate URL. If it's something like a logo change, the client might just update `software_version` to `2.0.1` and leave the URL as `2.0`. URL changes should really be reserved for things that would make a meaningful difference to an AS (but this is left up to the client implementer's judgment).

pulls.author: goutamadwant
pulls.body:
## Summary

- Require Client ID Metadata Documents not to derive their contents from untrusted external input, including URL components and request context.
- Preserve intentional operator updates, key rotation, and independently configured documents at distinct Client Identifier URLs.
- Document the tracking and selective-deception risks of requester-specific metadata, and recommend minimizing identifying information in metadata fetches.

## Rationale

A request-driven Client ID Metadata Document can allow an attacker to construct arbitrary security-sensitive metadata, or allow a client to present different identity or policy information to selected users and authorization servers. This makes independent review and moderation unreliable.

The change follows the direction discussed in #89 and addresses the related privacy and security concerns raised in #91 without preventing legitimate operator-managed updates.

- `make lint`

pulls.title: recommend that the client normalize its Client Identifier URL
pulls.author: kamronbatman
pulls.body:
The Client Identifier URL section states that `https://example.com/client` and `https://example.com:443/client` are not equivalent even though 443 is the default port for the `https` scheme. Under RFC 3986 they are equivalent: Section 3.2.3 directs URI producers to omit a port that is the same as the scheme's default, and Section 6.2.3 lists the two forms as equivalent. The two forms are also indistinguishable on the wire, since the default port is omitted from the Host header.

As settled in the discussion below, the authorization server continues to do strict string comparison and does no normalization. Instead, the client SHOULD produce a normalized Client Identifier URL, by reference to the syntax-based and scheme-based normalization in Sections 6.2.2 and 6.2.3 of RFC 3986, which cover the scheme and host case, the default port, dot-segments, and percent-encoding. The example is reworded as a consequence of comparison: a client that presents `:443` in one request and no port in another is treated as two different clients. No new references are added.

Earlier revisions of this PR had the authorization server normalize before comparing; that approach was withdrawn per the review.

Addresses the port question raised in Justin Richer's review, #79.

This PR was built with AI Assistance and has been thoroughly reviewed and authorized by Kamron Batman
